title: Nielsen's Heuristics
body:
Ten principles used as the checklist for [[Heuristic Evaluation]]. They are deliberately
broad, which is what makes them apply to interfaces nobody had imagined when they were written.

```
1.  Visibility of system status          keep the user informed, see Feedback
2.  Match the real world                 use the user's vocabulary, not the system's
3.  User control and freedom             provide an exit and an undo
4.  Consistency and standards            see Consistency and Standards
5.  Error prevention                     make the wrong action impossible
6.  Recognition over recall              show the options, do not require memory
7.  Flexibility and efficiency           shortcuts for experts, defaults for novices
8.  Aesthetic and minimalist design      every extra element competes for attention
9.  Help users recover from errors       say what went wrong and what to do
10. Help and documentation               available, searchable, task-oriented
```

Several restate constraints from [[Human Capabilities]] in design language. Number 6 is
the short-term memory limit. Number 8 is the attention limit. Number 1 exists because a user
with no [[Feedback]] cannot tell a slow system from a broken one.

Number 5 outranks number 9, and the ordering is the practical lesson: a well-worded error
message is worse than a design where the error cannot occur. Disabling what cannot be selected,
constraining input to valid values, and confirming a destructive action all prevent the error,
where a message only explains it.
